findings.headline: Capital financing is entirely internal; no external borrowing except one ageing PWLB loan
findings.detail: The council has one PWLB loan of £0.883m at 2.59% with 14 years to maturity. It is financing capital from internal cash reserves (£5.3m internal borrowing) and grants/capital receipts. The liability benchmark is negative (£31.752m), meaning the council does not currently need external borrowing. However, this model is vulnerable if cash reserves decline or internal borrowing costs rise.
findings.matters: A council wholly dependent on internal reserves for capital financing faces exposure to cash flow stress if planned underspends reverse, or if grants dry up. The risk assessment identifies 'Interest Rate Risk if Internal Borrowing is replaced by External Borrowing' — acknowledged as a live risk.
findings.figures: PWLB borrowing £0.883m at 2.59%, 14 years to maturity; internal borrowing £5.288m; total external debt £0.883m; liability benchmark (£31.752m)
findings.quote: It indicates that the Council does not currently need to externally borrow to fund its Capital Financing Requirement.

findings.headline: Strategic fund investments carrying book losses; volatility reserve covers only 98% of potential downside
findings.detail: Property and diversified income fund investments show a combined book loss of £0.419m (CCLA Property £0.225m, Ninety-One Diversified £0.360m, offset by Aegon gain £0.166m). The volatility reserve of £1.287m is earmarked to cover 98% of potential value reduction outcomes — a phrase that leaves 2% unhedged. The council transferred £0.183m out of the volatility reserve in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Strategic fund losses are eroding capital and the protection reserve is designed to cover only 98% of downside scenarios. If markets move adversely, the council could need to fund further losses from general reserves or reduce planned investment returns.
findings.figures: Strategic investments book loss £0.419m; volatility reserve £1.287m covering 98% of outcomes; transfer out 2025/26 £0.183m
findings.quote: Overall, in terms of strategic investments there is a 'book loss' of (£418,615) and the earmarked reserve to manage volatility risk is £1,286,791 to cover 60 out of 61 or 98% of potential value reduction outcomes

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered at 65% of approved budget, with material slippage on three major schemes
findings.detail: Capital expenditure was £15.8m against a revised approved budget of £24.3m (35% underspend). The largest variances were cinema development (£3.763m), social rented housing (£1.331m) and food waste collections (£1.281m). The paper states slippage can occur due to 'competing priorities for delivery teams, small delays leading significant budget slippage and often project delivery being subject to more complexities', but does not detail what has caused delays on these major schemes or when delivery is expected.
findings.matters: Large underspends and delays on capital schemes signal project management or resource constraints. The three-year pattern matters: this report compares actual 2025/26 to revised budget, not original budget, obscuring true trend.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £15.8m vs revised approved budget £24.3m (£8.5m or 35% underspend); cinema £3.763m, social housing £1.331m, food waste £1.281m
findings.quote: Slippage in capital spend is not uncommon and can be because of competing priorities for delivery teams, small delays leading significant budget slippage and often project delivery being subject to more complexities.

findings.headline: Cinema complex joint venture is generating losses, not the income assumed in the financial plan
findings.detail: The Darwin Prospects cinema joint venture made an operating loss of £0.158m in 2025/26 (£0.222m in 2024/25). The council's share was £0.079m. Only £3.315m of the £7.488m project budget has been spent; the council has not yet paid the second contribution (£1.589m) or food and beverage contribution (£1.700m). Income is assumed from 2028/29 onwards, but the joint venture is currently loss-making and loss is being carried forward.
findings.matters: A £11.487m commitment (including the approved £3.999m buyout option) is locking in capital and generating cash losses rather than the surplus assumed in the medium-term plan. This defers income by 2–3 years and depends on tenant take-up that has not yet materialised.
findings.figures: Cinema Complex Project Budget £7.488m, actual spend £3.315m to date; joint venture loss £0.158m in 2025/26 (£0.222m in 2024/25); council share £0.079m; total project budget including buyout option £11.487m
findings.quote: The Joint Venture Darwin Prospects LLP made an operating loss of £0.158m in 2025/26 (£0.222m in 2024/25) and the Council's share was £0.079m (£0.111m in 2025/26). This loss will be carried forward to later financial years and will be offset by income when tenants commence paying rent.

findings.headline: IT Change Management controls are not operating effectively
findings.detail: IT Change Management audit received a Limited assurance opinion, one of only two Limited opinions issued. This indicates system objectives are at risk due to non-compliance with key control procedures.
findings.matters: Weak controls over IT system changes can lead to unintended failures in financial systems, security compromises, or uncontrolled modifications to critical council applications.
findings.figures: Limited assurance opinion; 3 medium and 6 low-significance recommendations raised
findings.quote: we would draw attention to the Business Continuity and ICT change management reviews which were the only limited assurance opinions this year

findings.headline: Resource and capacity constraints evident across multiple service areas
findings.detail: Audits across several service areas identified resource and capacity constraints, with delays in providing audit evidence attributed to key contact workload.
findings.matters: Capacity constraints limit the council's ability to deliver improvements, respond to audit findings, and manage its financial commitments effectively, signaling potential vulnerability to unexpected demands.
findings.figures: Noted across 'several' service areas; not quantified specifically
findings.quote: Across several of the service areas reviewed, resource/ capacity constraints were evident. This was also apparent with delays in receiving evidence for some audits, due to capacity of key contacts.

findings.headline: Audit recommendations are stalling due to staff turnover and reassignment failures
findings.detail: As of February 2026, 34% of 98 outstanding audit recommendations were either partially implemented (21%) or not implemented (13%). A key issue identified was that original action owners left the council without reassigning recommendations to successors, requiring intervention from Internal Audit at Leadership Team level.
findings.matters: If audit recommendations aren't implemented promptly, control weaknesses persist. Staff departures without knowledge transfer suggest organizational churn and potential loss of institutional knowledge in finance functions.
findings.figures: 13% not implemented, 21% partially implemented, 7% not yet due (out of 98 actions as of February 2026)
findings.quote: A common theme was that the original action owners had left the organisation and the action had not been reassigned to an appropriate owner.

findings.headline: Payroll system lacks adequate segregation of duties
findings.detail: The payroll audit identified lack of segregation of duties as a high-significance weakness. Segregation of duties is a fundamental control to prevent error and fraud in financial processing.
findings.matters: Payroll is typically one of the largest budget areas; weak controls over who can initiate, approve and process payments creates risk of fraud, error, or unauthorized payments.
findings.figures: 1 high-significance finding raised in payroll audit; 4 medium and 2 low significance recommendations
findings.quote: the lack of segregation of duties noted in the payroll audit

findings.headline: Business continuity plans have not been completed across the council
findings.detail: The council was unable to provide completed business continuity plans for all services. This was flagged as a high-significance finding in the Business Continuity audit, which received a Limited assurance opinion—indicating system objectives are at risk and non-compliance with key procedures places the system at risk.
findings.matters: If the council cannot maintain critical financial and administrative functions during a disruption, it cannot reliably manage its finances or serve stakeholders, which directly affects the council's creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Limited assurance opinion (the only other Limited opinion was IT Change Management); classified as high-significance finding
findings.quote: High significance findings raised during the year were raised in relation to the lack of completion of business continuity plans across the council

findings.headline: Cinema complex joint venture making operating losses with only first tranche of funding spent
findings.detail: The cinema development joint venture (Darwin Prospects LLP) made operating losses in both 2025/26 (£158k) and 2024/25 (£222k), with the council's share being £79k and £111k respectively. Only the first contribution of £3.3m has been spent to date; the remaining £4.2m of the base project plus a further £4m buyout option remain unspent. No income is expected until 2028/29. The council's outstanding debtor to the JV is £3.7m.
findings.matters: This represents a substantial capital exposure currently delivering losses and behind schedule. Ongoing operating losses plus delayed revenue generation increase financial risk. Further capital requirements and extended payback extend exposure.
findings.figures: £3.3m of £7.5m base project spent, £11.5m total budget including buyout, £158k operating loss 2025/26, £79k council share, £3.725m long-term debtor to JV, no income until 2028/29
findings.quote: The Joint Venture Darwin Prospects LLP made an operating loss of £0.158m in 2025/26 (£0.222m in 2024/25) and the Council's share was £0.079m (£0.111m in 2025/26).

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by £8.5m (35% slippage), with cinema development completely unspent
findings.detail: The approved capital budget of £24.3m delivered only £15.8m actual spend, resulting in £8.5m slippage. Major items not delivered include cinema development £3.76m (0% spent), social housing £1.33m, and food waste collections £1.28m. All slippage is being carried forward to 2026/27, compressing future year budgets.
findings.matters: Large capital programme underspends indicate weak project forecasting or delivery problems. This affects the council's ability to deliver promised improvements and signals execution risk. Lenders are concerned about project management capability when budgets slip by a third.
findings.figures: £8,511,445 total slippage, £3,763,000 cinema (100% unspent), £1,331,589 social housing, £1,281,672 food waste, representing 35% of approved budget not delivered
findings.quote: The Capital Programme was (£8,511,445) lower than the Approved Budget on the cinema development (£3,763,000), social housing (£1,331,589) and food waste collections (£1,281,672).

findings.headline: Leisure centres overspent by £283k due to lower income and require ongoing financial monitoring
findings.detail: Leisure centres exceeded budget by £283k principally due to income shortfall of £18k and lower management company contribution of £219k. The council explicitly states this area requires ongoing review 'given the level of financial risk related to leisure centres'. The leisure centre earmarked reserve stands at £289k.
findings.matters: Leisure services are capital-intensive and heavily income-dependent. Persistent underperformance signals either weak demand/pricing or operational inefficiency requiring ongoing council subsidy, reducing overall financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £282,754 adverse variance, £18,091 income shortfall, £219,000 lower management contribution, £288,905 earmarked reserve as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Leisure centres were £282,754 higher than the Budget principally due to lower income. Budget performance will need to be kept under review given the level of financial risk related to leisure centres.

findings.headline: General reserves drawn down by £483k for Cabinet priorities not included in original budget
findings.detail: The council drew down general reserves to fund Cabinet priorities totalling £483k in 2025/26, compared to £0 budgeted in the original plan. This contributed to general reserves falling from the projected £5.8m to an actual £5.3m (total decrease of £539k). This represents discretionary use of reserves for non-essential items.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor reserve adequacy and trends closely. Drawing down reserves for unbudgeted priorities reduces financial resilience and flexibility to handle unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. It signals weaker financial discipline.
findings.figures: £483,374 used for Cabinet priorities, general reserves fell from £5.803m budgeted to £5.264m actual, total decrease £539,737
findings.quote: The actual use of general reserves in 2025/26 principally to fund Cabinet priorities of (£483,374) compared to the Original Budget of £0.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee Report on Proposed Accounting Policies Critical Judgements Estimation Uncertainty and Going Concern 2025_26 FINAL
findings.headline: Council commits to provide unconditional financial and operational support to subsidiaries LWM Traded Services Ltd (18 months minimum) and Darwin Prospects LLP (12 months minimum).
findings.detail: Council accounts will include group accounts incorporating LWM Traded Services Limited and Darwin Prospects LLP. The council will issue a letter of support to LWM Traded Services Ltd committing unconditional operational and financial support for at least 18 months from financial statement authorisation. For Darwin Prospects LLP, the council commits to provide support for at least 12 months and specifically to fund committed development works at the Three Spires Shopping Centre in Lichfield.
findings.matters: These are contingent support commitments that could require funding if subsidiaries encounter financial difficulties, particularly the shopping centre development which carries retail sector and development risk. The commitments extend beyond normal council operations and represent additional exposure for a lender.
findings.figures: LWM Traded Services Ltd: 18-month minimum support obligation; Darwin Prospects LLP: 12-month minimum support with Three Spires development funding commitment
findings.quote: The Council will provide a letter of support to LWM Traded Services Ltd that states that the Council will not withdraw its operations and continue to provide unconditional operational and financial support to LWM Traded Services Ltd for a period of no less than 18 months since the date of the authorisation of the financial statements of LWM Traded Services Ltd by its Directors.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee Report on Proposed Accounting Policies Critical Judgements Estimation Uncertainty and Going Concern 2025_26 FINAL
findings.headline: Staffordshire will be reorganised under Local Government Reorganisation in April 2028, with government's final decision expected May to June 2026.
findings.detail: The council states that Local Government Reorganisation needs consideration as part of going concern assessment. Staffordshire is in the second wave of reorganisations (April 2028). The council submitted detailed proposals on 28 November 2025, and statutory consultation closed 26 March 2026. Government is expected to announce its preferred proposal by summer 2026, with the Structural Change Order to be laid before Parliament by early 2027. The paper concludes going concern status is appropriate as the reorganisation is not until April 2028.
findings.matters: A lender must understand that this borrowing council will cease as a separate entity in April 2028, raising questions about debt succession, credit structure, and the duration of any lending relationship. The timing also creates near-term uncertainty until the government's decision is announced.
findings.figures: LGR second wave scheduled April 2028; government decision expected May–June 2026; Structural Change Order expected early 2027
findings.quote: Staffordshire will be in the second wave of councils to be reorganised in April 2028.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation 2026-27 will trigger Section 24 spending restrictions, constraining financial flexibility during transition
findings.detail: The council expects a Structural Changes Order and Shadow Authority elections in May 2027. The statement explicitly warns that Section 24 restrictions (spending limits) are routinely applied to reorganisation areas to protect the future authority's financial position. The council must maintain governance and controls during organisational transition and anticipated financial governance risks.
findings.matters: Section 24 restrictions directly limit a council's spending autonomy and borrowing capacity; reorganisation creates operational uncertainty and potential financial constraints during a period the council identifies as carrying high governance risk.
findings.figures: Structural Changes Order expected 2026-27; Shadow Authority elections expected May 2027; Section 24 restrictions anticipated
findings.quote: Managing financial governance risks and responding to any Section 24 restrictions that may be applied following the Structural Changes Order, as routinely occurs in reorganisation areas to protect the financial position of the future authority.

findings.headline: LWMTS traded services company governance weakened; external consultants commissioned to restructure oversight
findings.detail: The council's Lichfield West Midlands Traded Services Ltd has grown significantly, prompting external consultants (Fathom Consultancy, 2025) to recommend a shareholder advisory group to improve oversight. A Shareholder Advisory Group was established in September 2025. The LWMTS Board is recruiting non-executive directors to strengthen governance separation from shareholder roles.
findings.matters: Lenders need assurance that the council's commercial entities are properly governed and controlled; the need for external consultant intervention suggests prior governance gaps in a growing subsidiary.
findings.figures: Fathom Consultancy governance review commissioned 2025; Shareholder Advisory Group established September 2025
findings.quote: given the growth of LWMTS and other commercial relationships a governance review has been undertaken (Fathom Consultancy, 2025) and recommended that a shareholder advisory group would be beneficial, increasing consultation, oversight and transparency.

findings.headline: Audit Committee failed to reach quorum in December 2025, a core governance control now corrected
findings.detail: An Audit Committee meeting failed to reach quorum in December 2025 following a moved meeting date and member illness. External auditors had recommended ensuring strong member attendance and engagement on this key committee. The council has responded by changing Committee Membership and Vice-Chair appointments at Full Council in February 2026, plus additional member support measures.
findings.matters: The Audit Committee is the council's primary assurance mechanism for governance and financial control; quorum failure indicates temporary loss of independent oversight of risk and internal control.
findings.figures: one meeting failed to reach quorum, December 2025
findings.quote: a meeting failed to reach a quorum in December 2025. This was due to specific circumstances including the meeting having been moved and the health of one of the Members.

findings.headline: No provision made for Lichfield's share of Local Government Reorganisation implementation costs, and financial implications are unknown
findings.detail: The council states: 'It is unknown what financial implications will arise in the period prior to the new structure being implemented in 2028 or later' and explicitly confirms 'no provision has been made in the Revenue Budget for the Council's share of costs related to implementation.' This creates an unquantified liability in the final years before reorganization.
findings.matters: Reorganisation typically requires redundancy costs, IT system migration, legal work, and duplication of management during transition. The council is entering this period with rising deficits and declining reserves but no budget for these costs.
findings.figures: No figures. Cost of LGR implementation unquantified and unbudgeted.
findings.quote: It is unknown what financial implications will arise in the period prior to the new structure being implemented in 2028 or later. Therefore, at this stage, no provision has been made in the Revenue Budget for the Council's share of costs related to implementation.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing programme of £10.9m is concentrated in projects starting now, before reorganization
findings.detail: The council has identified borrowing need of £10.97m across the MTFS, primarily for replacement leisure centre (£5m), forward funding of capital projects pending receipts (£3.6m), social housing (£1.7m), and cinema development (£495k). These projects are being funded through internal borrowing and capital receipts, but all debt falls due before or shortly after the 2028 reorganization.
findings.matters: A significant capital programme is being financed during a period of shrinking reserves and growing deficits. The new unitary authority will inherit the debt repayment obligations alongside uncertainty over whether it will generate enough revenue to service them.
findings.figures: Total Borrowing Need: £10,972,000. Replacement Leisure Centre: £5,000,000; BRS projects forward funding: £3,636,000; Social Rented Housing: £1,741,000; Cinema development: £495,000
findings.quote: The Borrowing Need identified in the Capital Programme of £10,972,000 is related to: The approved new Leisure Centre - £5,000,000. Potentially forward funding the BRS projects temporarily using internal borrowing for up to three years pending the capital receipt being received - £3,636,000.

findings.headline: Food waste collection mandated from April 2026 with no confirmed central funding, creating revenue risk
findings.detail: A new statutory service to collect food waste from households begins in April 2026. The council has budgeted £1,500,000 in 2025/26 for operating this service, but the government has not separately identified funding. The document states: 'it is therefore not possible to confirm if the funding fully offsets the cost of this new service mandated by central Government.'
findings.matters: A large new service obligation (£1.5m+) is running on unconfirmed government funding. If actual costs exceed the government's unidentified allocation, the council absorbs the shortfall at a time when it's already facing deficits.
findings.figures: Food Waste Collection Cost budgeted at £1,500,000 for 2025/26; £1,550,000 for 2026/27; £1,600,000 for 2027/28
findings.quote: Revenue grant to operate the Food Waste Collection service from 1 April 2026 has not been separately identified and is therefore assumed to form part of Revenue Support Grant. However, it is therefore not possible to confirm if the funding fully offsets the cost of this new service mandated by central Government.

findings.headline: Business Rates reset redistributes all growth since 2013/14 and creates 'significant risk in business rate income projections'
findings.detail: The Final Settlement includes a full Business Rates Baseline reset with all growth since 2013/14 redistributed. The council's share of pooling gains was cut from 100% to 50% in the provisional settlement (later partially offset by a grant). The document explicitly states that changes to Business Rates Retention 'creates significant risk in business rate income projections'.
findings.matters: Business Rates income is now less predictable and lower after the reset, constraining revenue just as the council faces growing deficits. This is a permanent structural loss, not a temporary variance.
findings.figures: Business Rates Growth Allowance budgeted at £425,000 in 2026/27; Adjustment Support Grant (£245,000) in 2025/26 only to compensate for pooling changes
findings.quote: A full reset of Business Rates with all growth accumulated since 2013/14 redistributed within the sector. The approach to Business Rate Retention has been updated including how the Council's share of Business Rates is calculated in relation to reliefs, appeals and bad debts together with changes to the safety net and levy regime – this creates significant risk in business rate income projections.

findings.headline: Settlement funding depends on council maximizing Council Tax increases, and protection expires in 2029/30 creating a 'cliff edge'
findings.detail: The Final Settlement assumes councils will apply maximum Council Tax increases (3% for Lichfield, though the council only budgets 1.99%). Council Tax is expected to fund 74% of the settlement increase. The 95% income protection floor that provides a safety net only runs to 2028/29. The document explicitly warns of a 'cliff edge' risk when this protection ends.
findings.matters: If the council cannot or chooses not to maximize Council Tax increases, or if the new unitary authority harmonizes tax rates downward, the council's position becomes critically weak. The cliff edge in 2029/30 removes a key safety mechanism.
findings.figures: Settlement assumes 3% Council Tax increase (council budgets 1.99%); Council Tax funds 74% of settlement increase; 95% income protection runs only to 2028/29
findings.quote: This approach does however potentially create the risk of a 'cliff edge' in 2029/30 when the current three-year settlement ends.

findings.headline: Financial trajectory deteriorates sharply after 2026/27, moving from balanced budget to £2m+ funding gap by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council projects a balanced budget in 2026/27, then £657,000 gap in 2027/28 and £2,078,000 in 2028/29. General reserves fall from £5.2m at end-2025/26 to £2.4m by 2029/30, leaving minimal headroom above the £2m minimum. The trajectory worsens precisely as Local Government Reorganisation is happening.
findings.matters: A lender reviewing this council's medium-term viability would see a tightening position that coincides with organizational upheaval, reducing financial flexibility to weather setbacks.
findings.quote: A funding gap is projected from 2028/29 onwards and although this will be after Local Government Reorganisation is implemented, the Council should not take actions that negatively impact on the financial sustainability of the new authority.

findings.headline: Council is allocating £2.157m to address rising demand for temporary accommodation from cost-of-living crisis and refugee dispersal
findings.detail: The council has budgeted £2.157m to acquire residential properties for temporary accommodation and a further £2m for socially rented housing. The spending addresses increased demand driven by the cost-of-living crisis, rising Universal Credit claims, refugee dispersal, and increased unemployment and business closures placing sustained pressure on council services.
findings.matters: Rising demand for accommodation support is a structural cost pressure that could consume reserves and crowd out other priorities if economic conditions worsen.
findings.figures: £2.157m for residential property acquisition; £2m for socially rented housing delivery
findings.quote: The acquisition of residential properties with a budget of £2.157m to address the cost and demand of Temporary Accommodation.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is directly driving up the council's service disruption risk
findings.detail: Local government reorganisation (SR1) is the top strategic risk at 12/16. The impact cascades into service resilience: SR3 was specifically increased from 3 to 8 to reflect LGR's effect on capacity. The council notes risks to recruitment, retention, organizational morale, service delivery, and strategic partnerships during the reorganisation process.
findings.matters: Organizational disruption during LGR could impair the council's ability to maintain financial controls, deliver capital projects, or meet statutory obligations during a critical period.
findings.figures: SR1 Original 16, Current 12, Target 6. SR3 increased from score 3 to 8. £40k budget set aside for LGR work.
findings.quote: The current score for SR3 Resilience of Teams to effectively respond to a further disruption to services has been increased from 3 to 8 to reflect the impact Local Government Reorganisation could have on capacity.

findings.headline: Cyber-attack risk is the only strategic risk currently exceeding the council's risk appetite
findings.detail: Risk SR7 is scored at 8 (L2xI4), above the Averse appetite ceiling of 1-4. The council faces increasing sophisticated phishing attacks, remote working vulnerabilities, and persistent staff failures to complete mandatory ICT training or adopt multi-factor authentication. Successful attack could result in data loss, application unavailability, fines, and reputational damage.
findings.matters: A material cyber incident would compromise the council's control environment and operational continuity, affecting service delivery and financial reliability.
findings.figures: Original score 4 (L1xI4), Current score 8 (L2xI4). Multiple internal audits of cyber/IT controls rated at 'limited assurance' in 2024/25.
findings.quote: SR7: Threat to the Council's ICT systems of a cyber-attack remains the only risk which is currently outside of appetite.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio returns have halved, from 9% on historic cost (2024/25) to projected 3% (2026/27), due to retail asset value decline.
findings.detail: The council's property investment portfolio (78% retail, by historic cost) has seen net returns collapse. On historic cost basis, retail returned 3% in 2024/25; projected to fall to 3% in 2026/27. On current valuation, the decline is steeper: from 9% (2024/25) to 5% (2026/27). The fall is attributed to valuers using lower prevailing rental levels; retail property values fell from £9.68m (31/03/2023) to £4.64m (31/03/2025).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's major commercial asset class is in sustainable decline. Deteriorating returns may signal the need to divest or restructure the portfolio, or to accept permanently lower income from these assets.
findings.figures: Portfolio net return (historic cost): 2024/25 = 5%, 2026/27 = 3%. Retail property value: £9.68m (31/03/2023) → £4.64m (31/03/2025).
findings.quote: The value of these properties (mainly those classed as retail) have reduced because the value assessed by the external valuer is based on prevailing rental levels.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Food waste collections will cost £1.5m per year from 2026/27, a new unfunded revenue commitment.
findings.detail: The capital programme shows that food waste collection, beginning in 2026/27, will require £1.5m in that year and £1.55m–£1.648m in subsequent years. This is listed as a revenue implication of capital spend, but appears to have no corresponding savings or income identified in the budget. It is one of the largest single-year revenue pressures visible in the capital programme.
findings.matters: This is a legislated service but the council has not yet announced how it will fund this £1.5m+ annual cost. It will fall against a backdrop of declining investment income and draws on reserves, increasing debt or requiring spending cuts elsewhere.
findings.quote: Food Waste Collection 0 1,500 1,550 1,600 1,648

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Council is lending £7.488m to a joint venture company to develop a cinema, with indefinite repayment structure.
findings.detail: Lichfield has approved a capital loan of £7.488m (including £883k client contingency) to LWMTS (Lichfield West Midlands Trading Services) Limited to fund cinema development. This is in addition to equity investment of £225k in 2020/21. The loan appears with no specified repayment profile in the capital programme, only noting it will be "scheduled to be repaid after the expected date of the merger" under local government reorganisation.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the credit quality of the borrower (the council's own company), the collateral supporting this £7.488m exposure, and whether repayment is genuinely secured. LGR context suggests this is an orphan liability if reorganisation proceeds.
findings.figures: Cinema loan: £7.488m. Equity investment in LWMTS: £225k.
findings.quote: Council has approved a capital loan of £7,488,000 (including client contingency of £883,000) to the Joint Venture to deliver the Cinema development in Lichfield City.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement jumps to £14.689m in 2026/27, the highest in the forecast period.
findings.detail: The council's borrowing need (CFR) is projected to reach £14.689m in 2026/27, up from £11.086m in 2025/26, driven by three major capital projects: replacement leisure centre (£8.034m approved spend), cinema development (£8.108m total), and social housing (£2.742m). Despite this, external borrowing remains minimal at £0.823m; the gap is funded through internal borrowing.
findings.matters: This is the peak of the council's near-term capital ambition. If projects slip, costs overrun, or income sources fail (capital receipts, grants), the council will need to move from internal to external borrowing, triggering interest rate risk and debt servicing cost.
findings.figures: CFR 2026/27: £14.689m. External borrowing: £0.823m. Internal borrowing headroom: £10.628m.
findings.quote: The new leisure centre, the Cinema for Lichfield District and Socially Rented Housing will initially be funded through Internal Borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Investment balances declining sharply from £47.891m to £15.477m by 2029/30, reducing revenue available for services.
findings.detail: The council's treasury investment balance is forecast to fall by £32.414m over five years, from £47.891m in 2024/25 to £15.477m in 2029/30. This is because capital projects (leisure centre, cinema, housing) are being funded by drawing down cash balances rather than external borrowing. As balances fall, investment income—currently 10% of total funding—will decline correspondingly, creating a structural revenue pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this reserve drawdown is sustainable and when the council may exhaust liquidity, particularly if capital projects slip or face cost overruns.
findings.figures: Investment balances: £47.891m (2024/25) → £15.477m (2029/30). Gross investment income: £1,665,876 (2026/27), 10% of total funding.
findings.quote: The levels are projected to reduce due to the financing of the Capital Programme from earmarked reserves, grants and contributions and Internal Borrowing.

findings.headline: Cinema complex joint venture service investment is currently loss-making with £11.487m total approved budget including potential buyout
findings.detail: The council's joint venture investment in Darwin Prospects LLP cinema made an operating loss of £0.222m in 2024/25, of which £0.111m is the council's share. The council has already invested £3.315m in cash and transferred £0.410m of land value. An additional £3.999m budget has been approved for a potential buyout of the joint venture partner. Total project budget is £11.487m. Returns are currently treated as budget neutral pending better operating performance from the venture.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the council's substantial committed capital (£11.5m, or 35% of the original capital programme) tied up in a currently loss-making commercial venture with uncertain timing and magnitude of returns.
findings.figures: £11.487m total project budget, £0.222m operating loss in 2024/25, £3.315m cash invested, £0.410m land value transferred, £3.999m buyout budget
findings.quote: The Joint Venture Darwin Prospects LLP made an operating loss of £0.222m in 2024/25 and the Council's share was £0.111m. This loss will be carried forward to later financial years and will be offset by income when tenants commence paying rent. In addition, a budget to potentially buy out the Joint Venture partner of £3.999m has been approved by Council resulting in a total project budget of £11.487m.

findings.headline: Council faces growing medium-term financial challenge with uncertainty over key income sources and reserves vulnerable in downside scenarios.
findings.detail: The audit report identifies that 'The Council faces, over the medium term, growing financial challenge and increasing uncertainty over its longer-term income predictions' particularly around New Homes Bonus, Business Rates Reset, and Fair Funding Review. The pessimistic MTFS scenario projects general reserves declining to £4.423m by 2027/28 (from current £5.747m), representing potential £1.3m depletion in just 3 years.
findings.matters: Medium-term funding uncertainty combined with reserve depletion in downside scenarios could impact debt servicing flexibility and refinancing terms.
findings.figures: Pessimistic scenario: general reserves decline from £5.747m to £4.423m by 2027/28; net service expenditure 2024/25 was £13.731m
findings.quote: The Council faces, over the medium term, growing financial challenge and increasing uncertainty over its longer-term income predictions, particularly in respect of New Homes Bonus, Business Rates Reset, Fair Funding Review and Local Government Reform.

findings.headline: £70k capital investment in Darwin Prospects joint venture with governance reporting framework still being developed.
findings.detail: The council entered a joint venture (Darwin Prospects LLP) with Rookman Properties to redevelop the town centre shopping precinct. The council incurred £70k in costs relating to the cinema project during 2024/25. While structured as limited liability (council not exposed to net liabilities), the audit report notes that 'performance monitoring arrangements are being developed' rather than established, indicating incomplete governance framework during early stages.
findings.matters: New material capital investment in early-stage venture with governance reporting gaps creates execution risk and limits visibility into performance and costs.
findings.figures: £70k costs in 2024/25
findings.quote: In advance of the Joint Venture becoming operational, the Council incurred £70k in costs relating to the cinema project during 2024/25. Management has indicated the performance of the Joint Venture will be reported through appropriate channels which are being developed.

findings.headline: Council will be absorbed into unitary authority by April 2028, creating material uncertainty around financial sustainability and reserves.
findings.detail: The audit report identifies that local government reorganisation from 1 April 2028 creates 'significant change and uncertainty' over the next 2.5 years. Specific risks include loss of key individuals and corporate memory, incentive for short-term decision-making on reserve use, and the risk that accumulated reserves could be repurposed to cover overspends by the successor body. Management time will be diverted from realising savings plans.
findings.matters: Fundamental restructuring of the council creates uncertainty about debt servicing capacity, future revenue stability, and control over accumulated reserves.
findings.figures: 1 April 2028 (transition date)
findings.quote: Councils will need to consider the risk of the loss of key individuals and corporate memory in the lead-up to and transition into the new unitary authority. There may be an incentive for more short-term decision making in respect of the use of reserves and concerns, where reserves have been built up over previous years, either via strong management or for the implementation of a particular redevelopment scheme, that these reserves may end up being repurposed to cover an overspend incurred by a successor body.

news_drafts.headline: Capital financing is entirely internal; no external borrowing except one ageing PWLB loan
news_drafts.lead: A council wholly dependent on internal reserves for capital financing faces exposure to cash flow stress if planned underspends reverse, or if grants dry up. The risk assessment identifies 'Interest Rate Risk if Internal Borrowing is replaced by External…

news_drafts.headline: Strategic fund investments carrying book losses; volatility reserve covers only 98% of potential downside
news_drafts.lead: Strategic fund losses are eroding capital and the protection reserve is designed to cover only 98% of downside scenarios. If markets move adversely, the council could need to fund further losses from general reserves or reduce planned investment returns.

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme delivered at 65% of approved budget, with material slippage on three major schemes
news_drafts.lead: Large underspends and delays on capital schemes signal project management or resource constraints. The three-year pattern matters: this report compares actual 2025/26 to revised budget, not original budget, obscuring true trend.
